Automated PR Cleanup

Thank you for contributing to opencode.

Due to the high volume of PRs from users and AI agents, we periodically close older PRs using automated criteria so maintainers can focus review time on the most active and community-supported contributions.

This PR was closed because it matched the following cleanup criteria:

- The PR was created more than 1 month ago
- The PR had fewer than 2 positive reactions
- Positive reactions are counted as thumbs-up, heart, celebration, or rocket reactions on the PR

PRs created within the last month are not affected by this cleanup.

If you believe this PR was closed incorrectly, or if you are still actively working on it, please leave a comment explaining why it should be reopened. A maintainer can review and reopen it if appropriate.

Thanks again for taking the time to contribute.

This issue might be a duplicate of or closely related to existing issues not yet listed in your references. Please check:
- #29204: Memory leak in server mode via unbounded EventTarget listeners per session — the `MaxListenersExceededWarning` you observed in your logs is the same symptom reported there, and the root cause may overlap.

Also, the maintainers are tracking memory issues centrally in the **Memory Megathread** #20695, which includes instructions for capturing heap snapshots that would directly help diagnose this issue. If you can upload a heap snapshot following the instructions there, it would likely accelerate a fix.

Checked #29204 — we see the same `MaxListenersExceededWarning` from the Effect emitter (11 listeners, same stack shape, ours on 1.18.25 serve), so the in-process listener accumulation it describes is probably part of what we hit too.

One distinction worth keeping separate: in our case most of the 20 GB is external child processes, not core RSS. At the census point the `opencode serve` process itself was ~0.9 GB while the systemd unit (server + MCP children) held ~3 GB and was climbing ~300 MB/min via spawned MCP sets, about 100 processes at 70-100 MB each. Because core RSS stays under 2 GB for a long time on this path, the automatic heap snapshot flow (`OPENCODE_AUTO_HEAP_SNAPSHOT=1`, fires at 2 GB RSS) would likely never trigger for us.

If a heap snapshot of the serve process would still help, tell us which flow to use for headless serve — the manual ctrl+p flow looks TUI-side as far as we can tell — and we will capture one. We can also reproduce the child-process accumulation on demand.

Ran into this on 1.18.23 (headless `opencode serve`, systemd) and have numbers from the post-mortem, plus an angle we could not find elsewhere in this thread: the table does not just eat disk. The re-serialization work starves the event loop and kills HTTP while the kernel still accepts TCP.

Our DB reached 12.8 GB (11.2 GB of events, roughly ten days). Attribution:

- `message.updated.1`: 145,433 rows, 9.7 GB total, largest single event 29.1 MB
- `message.part.updated.1`: 379,175 rows, 919 MB
- `session.updated.1`: 39,679 rows, 28 MB

The big payloads embed the full message JSON including `summary.diffs` file patches. We caught one session live where a message jumped from 1.12 MB to 14.08 MB mid-stream, and the identical 14,079,136-byte `message.updated` payload was then persisted four more times verbatim (same length at seq 1085/1106/1122/1146). That mechanism is #42748, and it is what makes this table quadratic rather than just large.

The hang itself: during two concurrent streaming turns the server went near-silent. The kernel kept accepting connections on :4040 but HTTP was never serviced (curl code 000 at 5s, TTFB infinite). The process wrote another 536 MB over the following 40 minutes at a crawl, RSS around 7 GB, no error in the log at that point. Stopping the server, deleting the accumulated event rows and compacting the database (13 GB down to 1.2 GB) brought HTTP back instantly (200 in 1.3 ms), so the live churn was the killer, not the file size on disk.

Since the fix is tagged 2.0, we now keep it in check with a weekly cleanup that deletes the event rows of sessions nobody has touched for 48 hours (the server keeps running while it does). The table still accumulates on 1.18.25, though far slower since we turned snapshots off (see the correction below).

Correction, after dating every event by the timestamp embedded in the payload: an earlier revision of this comment claimed the 26-28 MB events kept occurring with snapshots disabled. That was wrong — those events were all written hours *before* we disabled the snapshot feature, and none after.

With the snapshot feature on, one day produced 7,920 `message.updated` events totaling 1.1 GB, single events up to 27 MB, and the same giant payload stored over and over. The day after disabling it (`"snapshot": false`): 10,509 events, 6.7 MB total, and not one event above 1 MB. So the diffs embedded in message summaries are tied to the snapshot feature, and turning snapshots off stops them entirely for us.

Sharing because it doubles as a stopgap for others hitting this: `"snapshot": false` in the config removed the giant payloads and the event-loop stalls that came with them. We lost the per-session change tracking, which we are fine without until the 2.0 fix.

Direct evidence of this from our 1.18.23 post-mortem, in case a concrete capture helps:

One session (glm-5.3, long streaming turn, large file edits in summary.diffs) had a message grow from 1,121,496 bytes at seq 1068 to 14,079,136 bytes at seq 1085. From that point on, the byte-identical 14 MB `message.updated` payload was persisted again at seq 1106, 1122, and 1146. Four writes of the same bytes, one per subsequent part mutation.

Table-wide this left 145,433 `message.updated.1` rows totaling 9.7 GB (max single event 29.1 MB) in a 12.8 GB opencode.db after about ten days. The downstream effect on a headless server (event-loop starvation until HTTP stops responding) is in my comment on #33356.

Another data point for this, with a failure mode I don't see covered in the existing reports: on a distro that puts a **per-user quota** on `/tmp`, this bug bites at **80% of the tmpfs, not 100%**, and it takes down **unrelated programs** rather than opencode itself.

### Environment

- opencode: `1.18.25` (standalone binary, `~/.opencode/bin/opencode`, 184 MB)
- OS: Fedora Linux 44 (KDE Plasma), kernel `7.1.10-200.fc44.x86_64`
- systemd: `259 (259.8-1.fc44)`
- Terminal: `xterm-256color`

### What accumulated

1010 byte-identical copies of the extracted library, ~6.2 GB total:

```
$ ls -1 /tmp/.*-00000000.so | wc -l
1010
$ du -shc /tmp/.*-00000000.so | tail -1
6,2G  total
$ md5sum /tmp/.9adb5ebfeaedff8f-00000000.so /tmp/.9adb5ef9ffe6ed87-00000000.so
d08bd9a52225cacba076f60cca5a697e  ...
d08bd9a52225cacba076f60cca5a697e  ...   # identical
$ objdump -p /tmp/.9adb5ebfeaedff8f-00000000.so | grep SONAME
  SONAME               libopentui.so
```

Each file is 13,745,312 bytes (13.10 MiB) — smaller than the ~21 MB reported in the issue body, so the size tracks the opentui/bun version. Timestamps spanned 19:48–22:59 on a single day: ~1010 launches accumulated in about three hours of normal use.

### Why the quota makes this worse

Fedora 44 ships systemd's stock `tmp.mount`, which enables tmpfs user quota:

```
Options=mode=1777,strictatime,nosuid,nodev,size=50%,nr_inodes=1m,x-systemd.graceful-option=usrquota
```

The default per-user limit is 80% of the filesystem. So on a 7.8 GB `/tmp` the ceiling is 6360 MB, and the leak hit it while `df` still showed 20% free:

```
$ df -h /tmp
tmpfs  7,8G  6,3G  1,6G  80% /tmp
$ quota -s -u <user>
     Filesystem   space   quota   limit   grace
          tmpfs  6359M   6360M   6360M
```

### The part that cost the most time to diagnose

opencode itself kept working. What broke was **everything else that writes to `/tmp`**, and it broke silently. Writes returned `EDQUOT`, which surfaced as shells that exit 1 with **empty stdout and empty stderr** — the failing component never got to report anything:

```
$ echo hello        # exit 1, no output
$ true              # exit 1, no output
```

`true` returning 1 is what finally gave it away: the shell was dying before executing anything, because its wrapper couldn't create a temp file. Any tool that stages work through `/tmp` shows the same shape — it just stops, with no error to search for. Tracking it back to opencode took reading `/proc/mounts` to spot `usrquota`, then `objdump -p` on one of the files to get `SONAME: libopentui.so`.

Worth noting for the fix discussion: `usrquota` on `/tmp` is stock systemd ≥ 256 behaviour, not a Fedora patch, so this "fails early and blames the wrong process" mode will get more common as distros pick up newer systemd.

### Confirming the files are orphans

None of the 1010 copies were mapped by any live process, so they are pure garbage rather than in-use libraries:

```
$ lsof /tmp/.*-00000000.so | wc -l
0
$ ls -l /proc/*/map_files/ 2>/dev/null | grep -c '00000000.so'
0
```

Deleting them reclaimed the full 6.2 GB and restored `/tmp` to 1% used, with no restart needed.

### Workaround

Since `r` lines in `tmpfiles.d` don't accept an age field and `systemd-tmpfiles --clean` doesn't process them, a `tmpfiles.d` rule alone can't express "delete files matching this glob older than N minutes". A systemd **user** timer works without root:

```bash
# ~/.local/bin/clean-opentui-tmp.sh
find /tmp -maxdepth 1 -type f -user "$(id -u)" -name '.*-00000000.so' -mmin +60 -print0 |
  while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
    lsof -- "$f" >/dev/null 2>&1 || rm -f -- "$f"
  done
```

driven hourly by `OnUnitActiveSec=1h`. The `-mmin +60` and `lsof` guards are belt-and-braces — deleting a mapped `.so` is safe on Linux, since the inode survives until unmapped — but they keep the purge from racing a launch that has just extracted its copy.

This issue might be a duplicate of existing issues. Please check:
- #34798: Conversations hang after first response when provider returns a `reasoning` field (using Ollama/Qwen3) — same root cause area: Ollama returns `reasoning` field but the openai-compatible provider only handles `reasoning_content`
- #43293: Ollama reasoning models hang or enter degenerate generation loops — related symptom from reasoning field mishandling via Ollama's OpenAI-compatible endpoint
- #37073: TUI final response missing after Thought block for reasoning models — same observable outcome (answer empty after reasoning block)

Yes, #46030  and #41033  describe the exact same problem! 

The model gets completely stuck in a text-only loop, endlessly narrating what it's about to do (like printing `Let me grep...` or similar tool intents as plain text) instead of actually emitting structured tool calls. This causes a massive token drain and spams the chat interface completely. 

Thanks for pointing those out — they match the symptoms spot on.

Thanks for tracking these down. To disentangle them — they're not really duplicates of each other, they're the different halves of the same feature:

- **#32370** (copy side): `linux_clipboard_selection` in `tui.json` (`clipboard`/`primary`/`both`, default `both`). Copy populates the configured buffer(s), and in `primary` mode TUI paste also *reads* the primary buffer. Also fixes `wl-copy` MIME detection.
- **#6370**: write-side only, opt-in (`enablePrimaryCopy`, default off), no read support. #32370's `both` default subsumes it.
- **#44938** (yours, paste side): middle-click reads the primary selection into the prompt. It doesn't change what the TUI writes on copy, so on its own the primary buffer is only populated by other apps or native terminal selection — it pairs with #32370 to complete the highlight-to-copy / middle-click-to-paste round trip.
- **#44443** is unrelated to clipboard buffers (selection → quoted context in the prompt).

So #32370 isn't duplicating #44938 or #44443 at all — the only overlap is #6370's write path, which it extends rather than repeats. Happy to merge in #44938's middle-click dispatch if/when the write side lands; the `ClipboardService` API in #32370 is structured to accept a `read(selection)` extension.

Fwiw, current `dev` has no primary-selection support yet, so one of these is still needed — and #6370 has been sitting since Dec 2025 and would conflict with either.
